question: What is the main job of glial cells in the nervous system?

question: Why does iron-deficiency anemia often leave a person feeling completely wiped out?

question: During a lumbar puncture, a patient suddenly moves and straightens their legs. What should the nurse do first?

question: What do we mean by the "psychosocial impact" of an emergency?

question: Which vaccines should nurses recommend to help protect patients against viral STIs and related long-term complications?

question: Why is male involvement important in family planning decisions?

question: What is a major problem caused by constant political leadership changes in public health?

question: What is the main job of antiemetic medications?

question: What is a basic rule of good manners when arriving at a patient's home?

question: Which of these is NOT a limitation or downside of retrospective research?

question: What is the primary benefit of cloud-based health records in modern medical practice?

question: A ward normally discharges 5 patients a morning, but today 12 left at once because a visiting consultant cleared them all. What kind of variation is this?

question: What is the main job of Antidiuretic Hormone (ADH) when your body needs to hold onto water?

question: What is the main job of a medication like loperamide?

options.A: Coating the stomach lining to prevent acid reflux
options.B: Stimulating water absorption by increasing salt intake
options.C: Killing all parasites living in the large intestine
options.D: Slowing down intestinal motility to reduce stool frequency

explanation: Loperamide calms down the bowel muscles (peristalsis) so a patient isn't running to the toilet quite as often. Simple and effective when used correctly! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T7#GNS212_U1_T7_h5)

question: What is a major challenge when you take a successful small test and try to use it across a whole hospital department?

options.A: The original nurses will refuse to share their secrets with others
options.B: Patients will automatically reject any change that originated outside their room
options.C: Different shifts may face unique conditions that cause the workflow to struggle
options.D: The hospital will immediately run out of paper charting supplies

explanation: What works smoothly during a quiet morning shift might totally jam up during a crazy night shift! Always expect to adapt when expanding your tests. [learn more](GST319_U3_T4#GST319_U3_T4_h6)

question: Which of these is a common interpersonal trigger for conflict among nurses on a unit?

options.A: Strict government healthcare regulations
options.B: The physical temperature of the nursing station
options.C: Poor communication and rushed handovers
options.D: The hospital's annual budget deficit

explanation: Rushed handovers and unclear messages easily lead to misunderstandings and hurt feelings between colleagues. Clear talk prevents unnecessary drama! [learn more](GST321_U5_T2#GST321_U5_T2_h3)

question: What is the standard temperature range for maintaining the cold chain in vaccine storage?

options.A: Plus 15 degrees Celsius to plus 25 degrees Celsius
options.B: Plus 2 degrees Celsius to plus 8 degrees Celsius
options.C: Plus 37 degrees Celsius to plus 40 degrees Celsius
options.D: Minus 20 degrees Celsius to minus 10 degrees Celsius

explanation: Most standard vaccines must be kept refrigerated between +2°C and +8°C to prevent them from spoiling. [learn more](GNS225_U2_T4#GNS225_U2_T4_h6)

question: What is another popular name for the ductus deferens?

options.A: Urethral tube
options.B: Vas deferens
options.C: Ejaculatory canal
options.D: Seminiferous duct

explanation: You will hear clinical instructors and textbooks use 'ductus deferens' and 'vas deferens' interchangeably. They are the exact same tube! [learn more](GNS121_U4_T2#GNS121_U4_T2_h4)

question: When should an intraosseous (IO) line be considered during resuscitation?

options.A: As the absolute first choice before trying any peripheral IV line
options.B: When the patient refuses to receive medications through the arm
options.C: Only after the patient achieves a return of spontaneous circulation
options.D: When intravenous access is difficult or taking too long to establish

explanation: IO access goes straight into the bone marrow and works as fast as an IV when placing a peripheral line fails. [learn more](GNS315_U4_T4#GNS315_U4_T4_h5)

question: How can a tele-nurse help assess a patient's physical status from afar?

options.A: Guessing the vital signs based on the patient's age
options.B: Relying entirely on laboratory tests done once a year
options.C: Guiding the patient or caregiver to perform simple checks at home
options.D: Physically walking to the patient's house for every assessment

explanation: You got it! You can coach the patient or a family member on how to check simple things like pulse rate or swelling at home. [learn more](GNS113_U1_T10#GNS113_U1_T10_h5)

question: Why would a nurse researcher choose a retrospective study to look into a very rare disease?

options.A: It costs nothing to access and analyze hospital databases
options.B: It proves the exact cause of the disease without any doubt
options.C: Past records already contain enough accumulated cases to study
options.D: Patients prefer answering questions about their past illnesses

explanation: Spot on! Because rare conditions take forever to pop up in real-time studies, looking backward at existing hospital records lets researchers gather enough cases right away. [learn more](GNS224_U1_T14#GNS224_U1_T14_h1)

question: Why is it usually unhelpful to just punish a nurse after a mistake happens on the ward?

options.A: It stops other staff members from documenting patient care properly
options.B: It ignores the underlying system flaws that allowed the error to happen
options.C: It makes the nurse work faster during the next emergency shift
options.D: It increases the budget available for buying new medical equipment

explanation: Exactly! Blaming just one person doesn't fix a broken system. To keep patients safe, we have to fix the root causes so the same mistake doesn't happen again. [learn more](GNS312_U5_T7#GNS312_U5_T7_h3)

question: How does keeping a patient close to your body help protect your back during a transfer?

options.A: It reduces the physical load and leverage on your spine
options.B: It makes the patient feel much safer and calmer
options.C: It prevents the patient from falling forward
options.D: It allows you to finish the hospital shift faster

explanation: Keeping heavy objects close to your center of gravity decreases the strain placed on your lower back muscles. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T25#GNS222_U1_T25_h3)
